description: A biomedical engineer who likes to take on challenges
summary:
AstroHealth is a working prototype of a self-monitoring health dashboard for crews on long-duration space missions. Built with .NET 8, Blazor WebAssembly and MongoDB Atlas, it lets each crew member keep an individual profile and log a quick check-in covering heart rate, blood pressure, glucose, oxygen saturation, temperature, sleep, mood and radiation dose.

It addresses the challenge of health risks in spaceflight, such as microgravity, isolation, a closed habitat and radiation exposure, where access to Earth-based care may be delayed. A server-side rules engine checks each entry against thresholds, records alerts, and assigns a Normal, Warning or Critical status. The crew can then review trends, history and body-system guidance that points them to mission medical protocols.

This matters because consistent data and visible trends can help crews notice changes early and decide when to seek follow-up. The prototype is not a diagnostic tool. Its thresholds are illustrative, its demo data is synthetic, and it needs clinical validation, security controls and sensor integration before real use.
details:
AstroHealth is a self-monitoring health dashboard for crews on long space missions (ISS, lunar and Mars profiles). A crew member selects their profile and logs a quick check-in. The form accepts partial entries across eight indicators: heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose, oxygen saturation, body temperature, sleep, mood and radiation dose. Fields that aren’t available can stay blank.

When a check-in is submitted, the API applies rule-based thresholds, for example heart rate under 50 or over 110 bpm, or sleep under 6 hours. It records any alerts and assigns an overall status: Normal for 0 alerts, Warning for 1–2, and Critical for 3 or more. The crew member can then review:

  • a dashboard with their latest vitals and attention points
  • a heart-rate trend chart and timestamped history
  • a body-systems map with non-diagnostic guidance

A flag is a prompt to review, not a diagnosis.

Benefits

  • Consistent, self-reported health data that is kept separate for each crew member, role and mission environment.
  • Visible trends instead of isolated readings, so changes are easier to spot.
  • Clear prompts for crew-medical follow-up when help from Earth may be delayed.
  • Honest design: it states what it doesn’t do, and demo data is clearly labeled as synthetic.

Intended impact

The aim is to help crews notice health changes earlier and support informed follow-up under spaceflight conditions such as microgravity, isolation, a closed habitat, and radiation exposure combined with distance from care. It is a prototype and not medical advice, a certified medical device, or an official NASA system. Its main impact is as a foundation for a future validated tool.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Client: Blazor WebAssembly on .NET 8, with the MudBlazor UI library
  • API: ASP.NET Core 8 with REST controllers, Swagger documentation, and a ThresholdEvaluator for the rules
  • Database: MongoDB Atlas using the MongoDB.Driver, with astronauts and health_readings collections
  • Language: C#, with HTTPS/JSON between client and API
  • Hardware: none. Readings are entered manually, and no wearable or cabin sensors are integrated yet.

How it is creative

  • It applies everyday health tracking to an extreme setting, with context tied to specific spaceflight risks. Each of the four risks (microgravity, isolation, closed habitat, radiation) is paired with what the app tracks for it.
  • The body-systems map gives crew members context and safety guidance without making a diagnosis.
  • Tracking mood and sleep alongside vitals treats wellbeing as part of crew health, not just physical readings.
  • The simple Normal/Warning/Critical status makes the data readable at a glance.

Factors the team considered

  • Safety: the thresholds and guidance are illustrative and need validation by aerospace clinicians before operational use. The UI directs users to mission medical protocols.
  • Data: demo readings are flagged as synthetic. Radiation dose is recorded but has no alert rule yet.
  • Security and privacy: profiles organize records and are not access control. Sign-in, authorization, audit and retention controls are planned, and credentials belong in a secret manager.
  • Realism: the prototype has no direct sensor feed, so integrating verified devices and resilient connectivity is a next step.
  • Next steps: bone-density and exercise tracking, radiation-dose rules, and testing of alert behavior, usability and deployment.
